events.title: Manco Inca's rising and the siege of Cusco
events.summary: Manco Inca, the Sapa Inca the Spaniards had crowned and then imprisoned and humiliated, escaped in April 1536 and laid a ten-month siege to Cusco, which the Spaniards held; when it failed he withdrew to Vilcabamba.
account: After Pizarro's men captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca and killed him in July 1533, taking a ransom of over 39,000 lb (18 t) of gold and silver, they captured Cusco on November 15, 1533 and had Manco Inca crowned. Real power rested with the Spaniards, who frequently humiliated him; Juan Pizarro imprisoned him after an attempted escape in November 1535.

Released in January 1536, Manco left Cusco on April 18, 1536, met his military chiefs at Lares, and gathered an army estimated at 100,000 to 200,000 men (some sources say as few as 40,000) around the city, held by 190 Spaniards and several thousand Indian auxiliaries. The Incas seized the fortress of Sacsayhuamán above the city on May 5, 1536; the siege began on 6 May and lasted until March 1537.

Manco coordinated it with a siege of Lima under his captain Quiso Yupanqui; the Incas defeated four relief expeditions sent by Francisco Pizarro, killing nearly 500 Spanish soldiers. When the siege failed, Manco withdrew to Ollantaytambo and then to the remote jungles of Vilcabamba, where he founded the Neo-Inca State in 1537.

events.title: The conquest of the Muisca and the founding of Bogotá
events.summary: From 1537 to 1540 Spanish expeditions under Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada conquered the Muisca of the central Andean highlands of Colombia, burned their Sun Temple, and founded Bogotá in 1538 as the capital of the New Kingdom of Granada.
account: The Muisca, the 'Salt People', lived in a loose confederation of rulers on the Bogotá savanna and the highlands of central Colombia, with an agriculture going back to around 3000 BCE; they traded gold, tumbaga and emeralds.

The conquest began in March 1537, when Quesada's greatly reduced troops entered Muisca territory at Chipatá. In April 1537 they beat the psihipqua Tisquesusa at Funza; in the Iraka Valley the iraca Sugamuxi fell, and the Sun Temple was burned by two of Quesada's soldiers in early September. On August 6, 1538 Quesada founded Bogotá as the capital of the New Kingdom of Granada; Tisquesusa's successor Sagipa allied with the Spanish that month. The conquest lasted until 1540.

events.title: Valdivia invades Chile and Michimalonco burns Santiago
events.summary: Pedro de Valdivia founded Santiago in February 1541 and forced the natives into gold mining; the toqui Michimalonco raised about 16,000 warriors and destroyed Santiago on September 11, 1541, fighting on until the Spanish controlled the central valleys at the end of 1543.
account: The conquest of Chile began with Valdivia's arrival in 1541; Spanish conquerors came with thousands of yanakuna from the subdued Inca territories and a few African slaves. Valdivia defeated the toqui Michimalonco, who had a couple of years before expelled the Incas from the north of the Mapuche lands, and founded Santiago on February 12, 1541. He organized the first distribution of encomiendas and of indigenous people among the Spanish settlers; since Chile was not as rich in minerals as Peru, the natives were forced to work on construction and in placer gold mining.

Michimalonco's brother Trangolonco revolted and destroyed the Spanish settlement at Marga Marga, and the chiefs of the Cachapoal, Maipo and Mapocho valleys gathered around 16,000 warriors. On September 11, 1541 Michimalonco carried out the Destruction of Santiago, with only a handful of Spaniards barely surviving, and then waged an 'empty war' of starving the Spaniards of food. The Spanish finished controlling the valleys of Cachapoal, Maipo and Aconcagua at the end of 1543; in 1544 Michimalonco, with Diaguita allies, tried to cut the land route to Peru and was defeated at Limarí. The same year the Arauco War with the Mapuche began at the Bío-Bío River.

events.title: Potosí and the mita: the silver mountain worked by forced labour

date.text: 1545 (Cerro Rico found); 1573 (Toledo's mita); to the 1603 report

events.place: Potosí (Upper Peru, today Bolivia) and the southern Andes
events.summary: Silver was found at the Cerro Rico of Potosí in 1545; from 1573 Viceroy Francisco de Toledo drafted one in seven adult native men into the mines through the mita, a forced-labour system under which many died and whole communities fled.
account: Diego Huallpa, an indigenous prospector, is credited with discovering the Cerro Rico in 1545. Potosí grew to more than 200,000 people, and the mountain produced an estimated 60% of all the silver mined in the world in the second half of the 16th century; the Spanish still say valer un Potosí, 'to be worth a Potosí'. From 1554 the patio process used mercury to extract the silver, and mercury poisoning took the lives of many in the refining.

The Spanish Crown repurposed the Andean mit'a in 1573. Under Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, sent to Peru in 1569, communities had to provide one seventh of their male labour force; the first mit'a recruits reached Potosí in 1573, and recruitment came to cover nearly 200,000 square miles of southern Peru and present-day Bolivia. Thirteen thousand men were conscripted each year. Mitayos carried loads of 100 to 300 lbs up ladders in narrow shafts; many died or were seriously injured, and assignment to the mines was considered worse than a death sentence.

Thousands fled their villages and forfeited their land to escape the draft; by the late 17th century Upper Peru had lost nearly 50% of its indigenous population compared with a little over a century earlier. A 1603 report counted 58,800 Indians working at Potosí, 5,100 of them mitayos. Potosí was a multiracial society of native Andeans, Spanish settlers and black slaves.

points: “What nation hath not had a part in her kingdom, and gotten of her spoils?” Every nation was paid with the silver of Potosí: from America to Japan they paid with the Spanish silver dollar, and every nation benefited from it, so nobody had a problem with hating us and destroying us.

Over 8 million miners died in Potosí between the 1500s and the 1800s. Friends do not do that to people: you kill 8 million miners to make money and start your whole global trade, and you call us your friends.

At Potosí the Spanish created the template for the modern economy, exploiting workers in one part of the world; the nations are still benefiting from our spoil today, as Europe still stands on Africa. Of a free woman Israel became a bondslave.

events.title: Lautaro and the Battle of Tucapel
events.summary: Lautaro, a young Mapuche taken captive as a boy and made Pedro de Valdivia's servant, escaped in 1551, led the Mapuche to victory at Tucapel on December 25, 1553, where Valdivia was captured and killed, and fought on until he was killed in an ambush in 1557.
account: Lautaro (c. 1534 – April 29, 1557) was captured by the Spaniards at the age of 11 and forced into servitude as Valdivia's personal servant, later his stableman; there he saw that the conquistadors and their horses were only mortal. According to several historians, Valdivia ordered his men to cut off the feet and hands of every Mapuche in the tribe of Lautaro's father Curiñancu, among them his parents, for resisting colonization.

Lautaro escaped in 1551 and was declared toqui. In December 1553 the Mapuche destroyed the fort of Tucapel; on Christmas Day, December 25, 1553 they surrounded Valdivia, who had left Concepción with only 50 soldiers, and the battle ended in his capture and death. A typhus plague, drought and famine kept the Mapuche from driving the Spaniards out in 1554 and 1555; in 1556–1557 Lautaro tried to reach Santiago to free central Chile and was killed in an ambush in 1557. He is revered among Mapuche and non-Mapuche Chileans and Argentinians.

events.title: The fall of Vilcabamba and the beheading of Túpac Amaru
events.summary: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo declared war on the last Inca state at Vilcabamba in April 1572; its last ruler, Túpac Amaru, was hunted down, tried and beheaded in the main square of Cusco on September 24, 1572, ending the Inca state.
account: The Neo-Inca State founded by Manco Inca at Vilcabamba in 1537 lasted until 1572. When two Spanish ambassadors were killed on its border, Toledo declared war on 14 April 1572; the Spanish entered the deserted city on 24 June. Túpac Amaru fled into the lowland forests with about 100 people, and a group of forty soldiers under Martín García Óñez de Loyola pursued and arrested him with his wife.

The captives were marched into Cuzco on 21 September with the mummified remains of Manco Cápac and Titu Cusi. Five Inca generals were sentenced to hanging; Túpac Amaru was convicted of the murder of priests and sentenced to be beheaded. Clerics pleaded on their knees that he be sent to Spain instead, and Philip II disapproved of the execution. Before 10,000 to 15,000 witnesses in the main square of Cuzco, his reported last words were: 'Pacha Kamaq, witness how my enemies shed my blood.'

events.title: Curalaba and the destruction of the Seven Cities
events.place: Southern Chile, south of the Biobío River
events.summary: On December 23, 1598 the Mapuche vice toqui Pelantaru ambushed and killed the Spanish governor at Curalaba; in the uprising that followed the Mapuche and Huilliche destroyed or forced the abandonment of all seven Spanish cities south of the Biobío, ending the conquest period in Chile.
account: The revolt was triggered by the Battle of Curalaba on 23 December 1598, where Pelantaru and his lieutenants Anganamón and Guaiquimilla, with three hundred men, killed Governor Martín García Óñez de Loyola and nearly all his companions.

Over the next years the Mapuche destroyed or forced the abandonment of Santa Cruz de Coya (1599), Valdivia (1599, reoccupied in 1602 and abandoned again in 1604), Los Infantes (1599), La Imperial (1600), Villarrica (1602), Osorno (1603) and Arauco (1604). The chronicler Alonso González de Nájera wrote that more than 3,000 Spaniards were killed and over 500 women taken captive. The destruction gave rise to a Spanish–Mapuche frontier and, in traditional Chilean historiography, marks the end of the conquest.

events.title: Benkos Biohó and the maroons of Cartagena
events.place: Montes de María and La Matuna, near Cartagena de Indias, Colombia
events.summary: Benkos Biohó, an African sold at Cartagena in 1596, escaped in 1599 into the marshes and built a maroon army and palenque that the governor could not defeat; Spain made peace with him in 1605–1612, then seized him in 1619 and hanged and quartered him in 1621.
account: Biohó, described as of Mandinka origin from Guinea-Bissau, was seized by the Portuguese slave trader Pedro Gomes Reinel and sold in 1596 in Cartagena de Indias to Alonso del Campo. He escaped when the boat carrying him down the Magdalena River sank, was recaptured, and escaped again in 1599 into the marshy lands southeast of Cartagena with about 30 runaways. The maroons defeated the first expedition of 20 armed men sent against them, and Biohó came to dominate the Montes de María, taking the title 'king of Arcabuco' and organizing an intelligence network to help more slaves escape.

On 18 July 1605 Governor Gerónimo de Suazo y Casasola, unable to defeat the maroons, offered a treaty recognizing the autonomy of the Matuna palenque; peace was finalized in 1612. The Spaniards broke the treaty in 1619 when they captured Biohó in the city, and he was hanged and quartered on 16 March 1621; the governor argued that it was dangerous how much he was respected. By the end of the 17th century the Montes de María held over 600 maroons.

events.title: Cartagena de Indias, the slave port of New Granada

date.text: 1615–1654 (Claver's ministry); the Inquisition set up in Cartagena in 1610

events.summary: By the 17th century Cartagena de Indias was a key port for importing enslaved Africans under the asiento; about 10,000 captives were landed there each year, after a crossing in which an estimated one third died, and the Jesuit Peter Claver met the ships from 1615 to 1654.
account: Cartagena was a key port for the export of Bolivian silver to Spain and the import of enslaved Africans under the asiento system: Spain, the only European power with no trading posts in Africa, licensed merchants of other nations to bring slaves to its colonies. Pedro de Heredia, who entered the Bay of Cartagena on 14 January 1533, brought the first enslaved people to work clearing the underbrush; by the 17th century Cartagena was an important slave market, centered on the Plaza de los Coches. The Holy Office of the Inquisition was established there in 1610 and abolished with independence in 1811.

Peter Claver arrived in Cartagena in 1615 to work under Alonso de Sandoval, who had served the slaves for 40 years. Cartagena was a slave-trading hub where 10,000 slaves poured into the port yearly, crossing from West Africa under conditions so foul that an estimated one third died in transit. In 1622 Claver signed his profession 'Peter Claver, servant of the Ethiopians forever'; in 40 years he is estimated to have baptized around 300,000 people. He died on 8 September 1654.

points: The history of Spanish enslavement of Africans began with the Portuguese captains Antão Gonçalves and Nuno Tristão in 1441: the transatlantic slave trade did not start in 1619. They say that date to throw us off.

From 1595 to 1640 the transatlantic slave trade to the Spanish Americas was concentrated in a few American ports, Cartagena de Indias and Veracruz among them. Spain and Portugal made us slaves, and school and church will not teach it.

events.title: The slave trade through Buenos Aires and Montevideo
events.place: Río de la Plata: Buenos Aires and Montevideo
events.summary: Between 1680 and 1812, when the traffic was halted, more than 110,000 enslaved Africans were brought into the Río de la Plata through Buenos Aires and Montevideo, many of them sent on to the interior provinces and to Brazil.
account: The slave trade flourished through the port of Buenos Aires, where thousands of Africans arrived to be sold, many sent on to Brazil through a slave-smuggling network; most of those kept were sent to the interior provinces, while the Buenos Aires neighbourhoods of San Telmo and Monserrat housed many slaves.

From 1680 to 1777 at least 40,000 slaves were brought to the region; between 1777 and 1812, when the trafficking was halted, some 70,000 more were landed in Buenos Aires and Montevideo, besides an unknown number brought overland from Rio Grande do Sul. In the 18th and 19th centuries Black Argentines made up as much as half the population of some cities: 54% in Santiago del Estero, 52% in Catamarca, 46% in Salta, 44% in Córdoba and Tucumán.

events.title: San Basilio de Palenque wins its freedom
events.place: San Basilio de Palenque, near Cartagena, Colombia
events.summary: After decades in which its maroons freed Africans landed at Cartagena, the palenque of San Basilio was granted its freedom and its land by the Spanish Crown on condition that it take in no new runaways; the accord of 1713 made it the first free African town in the Americas.
account: The maroon community, made up of Africans and creoles from other nearby palenques, tried to free all the enslaved Africans arriving at Cartagena and was quite successful. The Spanish Crown issued a Royal Decree in 1691 guaranteeing freedom to the Africans of the palenque if they stopped welcoming new escapees, but runaways kept coming; the colonial authorities put down another rebellion there in 1696.

In January 1713, when it had 137 homes, the palenque was renamed San Basilio Magno. That year, after a prolonged period of fighting, Bishop Antonio María Casiani signed an accord granting the runaways the right to their land on condition that they accept no new maroons, which the Palenqueros eventually refused to honour. In 1772 it was included in the Mahates district. San Basilio de Palenque was declared a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2005.

events.title: The Guaraní War over the seven missions
events.place: Misiones Orientales, east of the Uruguay River
events.summary: When the 1750 Treaty of Madrid gave the seven Jesuit missions east of the Uruguay River to Portugal, their Guaraní refused to leave; a joint Spanish–Portuguese army defeated them at Caiboaté on February 10, 1756, killing 1,511 Guaraní for four European dead.
account: The Treaty of Madrid set the Uruguay River as the border between Spanish and Portuguese territory, and the seven missions east of it, with 26,362 inhabitants by a Jesuit census, were to be dismantled and moved west. For most of the missions' history the Guaraní had fought Luso-Brazilian slavers, the bandeirantes, who sought to capture them to sell in Brazil.

In 1754 the Jesuits surrendered the missions, but the Guaraní, led by Sepé Tiaraju, refused to relocate; Spanish and Portuguese forces sent in July 1754 failed to remove them. On 10 February 1756, 3,000 Spanish and Portuguese soldiers fought the Guaraní at Caiboaté: 1,511 Guaraní were killed and four Europeans. The army occupied the seven missions; Spain and Portugal annulled the treaty in 1761.

events.title: The rebellion of Túpac Amaru II

date.text: 4 November 1780 – 1783; Túpac Amaru II executed 18 May 1781

events.place: Cusco, Tinta and the southern Andes, Peru
events.summary: In November 1780 the kuraka José Gabriel Condorcanqui, taking the name Túpac Amaru II, led Quechua, Aymara and mestizo rebels against Spanish rule and the forced labour of the mita; he was captured and torn apart in Cusco on May 18, 1781, and the rising went on to 1783 at a cost estimated at 100,000 indigenous dead.
account: The rebellion arose against the Bourbon Reforms, which among other things forced the indigenous population to mine under the mita, largely at the Cerro Rico of Potosí; among Túpac Amaru II's proclamations were the freedom of the indigenous people and the abolition of slavery. It began on 4 November 1780 with the seizure of the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga, hanged on 10 November before thousands.

Betrayed after defeats at Combapata and Checacupe in April 1781, Túpac Amaru II was sentenced on 15 May and on 18 May forced to watch the execution of his wife, Micaela Bastidas, and one of his children; four horses failed to tear his limbs apart, and he was beheaded in the Plaza de Armas of Cusco. His relatives and Túpac Katari carried on until 1783. The death toll is estimated at 100,000 indigenous people and 10,000–40,000 non-natives. It was the largest revolt in the Americas before the Spanish American wars of independence and the Haitian Revolution.

events.title: Túpac Katari and the siege of La Paz
events.place: La Paz and El Alto, Upper Peru (Bolivia)
events.summary: The Aymara leader Túpac Katari raised some 40,000 men and besieged La Paz from March 1781; the siege was broken in October, and he was captured and executed by quartering in November 1781, with his wife Bartolina Sisa and his sister Gregoria Apaza later executed too.
account: Julián Apasa took the name Túpac Katari to honour the rebels Tomás Katari and Túpac Amaru. In 1781 he raised an army of some 40,000 and laid siege to La Paz on 13 March, holding court with his wife Bartolina Sisa in El Alto; the first siege lasted 109 days, from March until June, and the city held out with troops sent from Buenos Aires.

By 5 August he besieged the city again, joined by Andrés Túpac Amaru; the siege was broken by royalist forces on 17 October 1781. Betrayed by some of his followers, he was captured on the night of 9 November and executed by quartering. His reported last words were 'I die but will return tomorrow as thousand thousands'. Bartolina Sisa and Gregoria Apaza were also executed. In 2005 Bolivia declared Julián Apaza and Bartolina Sisa national Aymara heroes.

events.title: José Leonardo Chirino's rising at Coro
events.summary: In 1795 the free zambo José Leonardo Chirino, who had been to Saint-Domingue, led a rising at Coro for a republic, the freedom of all enslaved Africans and the end of native tribute; it was crushed, his children were sold into slavery, and he was executed in December 1796.
account: 1795 saw rebellions across the Caribbean, from Grenada to Jamaica, with the Haitian Revolution under way since 1791. Chirino (1754–1796) had recently travelled to Saint-Domingue; with José Caridad González, a Congolese man, he led the Coro rebellion.

Its four aims were an independent democratic republic without monarchy or colonialism, the freedom of all enslaved Africans and the abolition of slavery, the abolition of the tribute imposed on the indigenous population, and the abolition of privilege and prejudice by skin colour. After the rising was suppressed Chirino was betrayed by an associate and condemned to death; his children were sold into slavery, and he was executed on December 10, 1796.

events.title: Freedom of wombs and abolition in Chile and Argentina
events.summary: Chile freed the children of slaves in 1811 and abolished slavery in 1823, the second country in the Americas after Haiti; Argentina's Assembly of the Year XIII freed the wombs in 1813, but slavery was not abolished there until the constitution of 1853.
account: In Chile, Afro-Chileans numbered 20,000 by 1590 but only 4,000 at emancipation. With the freedom of wombs, slavery was stopped in 1811, and by 1823 Chile was the second country in the Americas to prohibit slavery, after Haiti, freeing close to five thousand slaves.

In Argentina the Assembly of the Year XIII, called in 1813 to establish the new state, passed the law of freedom of wombs, by which children born to slaves were free, but it did not free those already enslaved. Forty years later, in 1853, the constitution abolished slavery completely; universities did not admit Black people until then. Black men served in the Regimiento de Pardos y Morenos, which gained regimental status in 1810 and fought in the war of independence.

events.title: Bolívar's pledge to Pétion and the slow end of slavery from Venezuela to Peru
events.place: Haiti, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Paraguay
events.summary: In 1816 Simón Bolívar won arms and money from Haiti's president Alexandre Pétion by pledging to free the slaves of the lands he took; yet the republics freed only the newborn at first, and slavery lasted until 1851 in Colombia and Ecuador, 1854 in Venezuela and Peru, and 1869 in Paraguay.
account: Forced into exile on Jamaica after Spanish forces subdued New Granada in 1815, Bolívar reached Les Cayes in Haiti on 24 December and met Pétion on 2 January 1816; after he pledged to free every slave in the areas he occupied, Pétion gave him money and military supplies. Realising the importance of Black soldiers, Bolívar declared the abolition of slavery in 1812 and again in 1816.

After independence, the Congress of Cúcuta (1821) passed a law of free womb, manumission and abolition of the slave trade for what is now Colombia and Venezuela. Slavery was finally abolished in Colombia in 1851 and in Ecuador in 1851; in Venezuela on 24 March 1854, when fewer than 24,000 slaves remained; and in Peru in 1854 by President Ramón Castilla. events.title: The Occupation of Araucanía
events.summary: From 1861 to 1883 Chilean soldiers and settlers advanced into the Mapuche lands of Araucanía, independent through the whole colonial era, and incorporated them into Chile; thousands of Mapuche died by war and disease, chiefly smallpox, and their lands were reduced, plunging many into lasting poverty.

For ten years (1861–1871) the Mapuche could not stop the advance; the war brought famine in the winter of 1869, worsened by smallpox. After a decade of near peace, while Chile fought Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific, a large Chilean army reached the Cautín River in March 1881; a last coordinated Mapuche rising in November 1881 was defeated within days. The conflict killed thousands of Mapuche by warfare and disease, primarily smallpox, and the pillaging of the army and bandits and the reduction of their lands plunged many into poverty that has persisted for generations. It ran alongside Argentina's campaigns against the Mapuche of 1878–1885.

events.title: Colombia's 1991 constitution and the law for Black communities
events.summary: Colombia's constitution of July 1991 ended the definition of the nation as Catholic, Hispanic and Spanish-speaking and recognized its multiethnic and multicultural make-up, giving indigenous, Afro-Colombian and Raizal peoples legal and political recognition; under its Article 55, Law 70 of 1993 followed for the Black communities.
account: The constitution, promulgated on 7 July 1991 under President César Gaviria, replaced that of 1886 amid unprecedented violence. Colombia had been defined in exclusionary terms as a Catholic, Hispanic and Spanish-speaking nation; the 1991 constitution recognized its multiethnic and multicultural composition and allowed indigenous, Afro-Colombian and Raizal minorities to gain political, legal and cultural recognition.

Following the constitution, particularly Article 55, Law 70 of 1993 created within the Ministry of the Interior the Directorate for Black Communities, to form public policy and uphold the equality, identity and cultural autonomy of Black communities; with a 1995 education decree it opened the way to Afro-Colombian studies. Afro-Colombians remain among the most affected by the armed conflict: more than 2 million have been displaced.

events.title: The forced sterilization of Indigenous women in Peru
events.summary: Under President Alberto Fujimori, Peru's National Population Program sterilized an estimated 300,000 people between 1996 and 2000, chiefly poor Indigenous women of the Andes, often without their informed consent.
account: The campaign drew on eugenic and neo-Malthusian ideas set out in Plan Verde, a military strategy conceived during the internal conflict, which presented Indigenous populations as an obstacle to national progress and linked racial improvement with whiteness. Under Fujimori (1990–2000) these ideas became a systematic policy said to reduce poverty and high birth rates.

Between 1996 and 2000 an estimated 300,000 sterilizations took place, mostly of native women in rural Andean regions, often without informed consent, reflecting the belief that they were 'unfit' for reproduction.

events.title: Evo Morales and the Plurinational State of Bolivia
events.summary: Evo Morales, an Aymara former coca grower, won 53.7% of the vote in 2005 and became Bolivia's first president from its indigenous population; a new constitution approved by 61.43% of voters on January 25, 2009 made Bolivia a Plurinational State.
account: Born to an Aymara family of subsistence farmers, Morales rose as a leader of the coca growers and campaigned for indigenous and poor communities. Elected in 2005 with 53.7% of the vote, he was widely described as Bolivia's first Indigenous leader, at a time when about 62% of the population identified as indigenous, and was crowned Apu Mallku of the Aymara at Tiwanaku in January 2006. He served from 2006 to 2019.

The constitution approved in a referendum on 25 January 2009, with 61.43% of the vote and 90.24% participation, and adopted on 7 February 2009, converted the Republic of Bolivia into the Plurinational State of Bolivia, recognizing the self-determination of the nations within it.

events.title: The Baguazo: Awajún and Wampis blockade at the Devil's Curve
events.summary: On June 5, 2009 Peruvian security forces broke an Awajún and Wampis road blockade near Bagua, held against free-trade decrees opening the Amazon; at least 31 people were killed at the 'Devil's Curve', and nine more police died the next day at an oil facility.

On 5 June 2009 over 600 police dispersed several thousand Awajún and Wampis with tear gas and live ammunition; at least 31 people were killed.

On 6 June nine more police officers were killed at a Petroperú facility the protesters had seized. Not since the conflict with the Shining Path had so many died in such clashes in Peru. Within a week Congress suspended two of the decrees, and they were later repealed.

events.title: The Venezuelan exodus
events.summary: The crisis in Venezuela under Hugo Chávez and Nicolás Maduro drove the largest recorded refugee crisis in the Americas: over four million had left by mid-2019 and, by the UNHCR's count, more than 7.9 million in all.
account: Venezuelans wishing to emigrate rose from 30% in December 2015 to 57% in September 2016. By mid-2019 over four million had left since 1999, most in the preceding three and a half years; estimates reached 7.1 million by October 2022, over 20 percent of the population. The UNHCR counts more than 7.9 million emigrants; 390,000 left between May and August 2023 alone, driven by low wages, inflation, the lack of public services and political repression.

It is the largest recorded refugee crisis in the Americas and one of the most underfunded in modern history. According to a 2019 report by Mark Weisbrot and Jeffrey Sachs, the U.S. sanctions, which began in the 2010s, caused Venezuela a loss of $38 billion between 2016 and 2019 and, with preexisting trends, an estimated 40,000 excess deaths in 2017–2018.

events.title: Colombia's peace agreement with the FARC
events.summary: After the first peace deal with the FARC was narrowly rejected in a referendum on October 2, 2016, a revised agreement was signed on November 24 and ratified by Congress on November 29 and 30, officially ending the conflict that began in 1964.

events.title: The Mapuche conflict, Catrillanca, and the rejected plurinational constitution
events.summary: Mapuche communities' struggle for their ancestral lands, lost in the Occupation of Araucanía, sharpened after police shot Camilo Catrillanca in 2018 and Chile sent troops to Biobío and Araucanía in 2021; in 2022 voters rejected, 61.89% to 38.11%, a constitution that would have made Chile a plurinational state.
account: The Mapuche conflict intensified with the return of democracy in the 1990s, as activists sought to recover the 'ancestral territory' lost in the Occupation of Araucanía and the Conquest of the Desert; its period of violence began in December 1997, and some groups have used violent tactics since 1998 while others negotiate. In 1993 the Chilean government passed the Indigenous Peoples Act recognizing Mapuche land, cultural and development rights. In 2018 Camilo Catrillanca, grandson of a local Indigenous leader, was shot in the head during a police operation near Ercilla; in October 2021 President Sebastián Piñera declared a state of emergency and deployed troops to Biobío and Araucanía.

The constitution drafted after the 2020 plebiscite declared that 'Chile is a Plurinational and Intercultural State'; the plurinational state and indigenous justice were among its most debated provisions. On 4 September 2022 it was rejected by 61.89% to 38.11%, winning also in communes with large indigenous populations, and the 1980 constitution of the dictatorship era remained in force.

events.title: The Sacaba and Senkata massacres
events.summary: In the crisis after Evo Morales's fall in November 2019, soldiers and police fired on pro-Morales protesters, killing eleven coca growers' demonstrators at Sacaba on November 15 and ten demonstrators and bystanders at Senkata on November 19; the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights called Sacaba a massacre.
account: On 15 November 2019 Bolivian soldiers and police broke up a protest led by coca growers at Huayllani in Sacaba municipality, Cochabamba; eleven demonstrators were killed and about ninety-eight wounded. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights denounced the Sacaba events as a massacre in December 2019, and the experts it appointed ratified that description in their 2021 report.
